briefs.headline: AI corners 80% of all global equity funding in March quarter
briefs.deck: Global funding for AI reached a remarkable $226 billion by the end of March this year, accounting for nearly eighty percent of the total equity funding landscape. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic attracted significant investments earlier this year, but they are also facing increasing scrutiny regarding ethical considerations and the risks associated with AI technologies. Investors are now…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Whether AI will get us all killed by the end of the decade is still a matter of debate, but funding into artificial intelligence continues to soar.
In fact, it is only getting bigger. Global AI funding touched a whopping $226 billion in the March quarter this year. That's almost 80% of all global equity funding, showed a study by Boston Consulting Group (BCG). This pie stood at 41% in the year-ago period and at just about 15% in CY2022, explaining the pace at which investor dollars are chasing AI. American AI giants 
OpenAI
 and Anthropic have contributed to the bulk of this investment surge with their massive fundraises earlier this year. In March, OpenAI raised $122 billion at a post-money valuation of $852 billion while Anthropic bagged $30 billion in capital from investors in Feb at a valuation of $380 billion.
Call it ironical or not but both Anthropic and OpenAI which are at the forefront of AI innovation have come under scrutiny for unethical practices. Earlier this week, Jacob Coxon, a researcher with Anthropic, quit the firm, raising concerns over the risks that come with the unfettered rise of AI. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives....the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon said on X.
About 65% of AI equity funding has been cornered by foundation models and platforms in 2026 (Jan-Jun period), up from a mere 4% in 2022. "Investors are concentrating bets on the intelligence layer of the AI stack," analysts at BCG said.

briefs.headline: FM calls for tech body for stronger global voice
briefs.deck: In a bold move for India's tech sector, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has unveiled a federated industry platform designed to amplify the industry's global presence. This platform will proactively liaise with international governments and regulators while fostering collaboration on data and cybersecurity standards. The goal is to equip Indian companies with the tools needed to confidently…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Finance minister 
Nirmala Sitharaman
 called upon tech companies to promote a federated industry platform to give India's technology sector a stronger collective voice in global markets and regulatory discussions.
"There may be merit in considering a federated industry platform that brings together the broader Indian technology ecosystem," Sitharaman said at Global Fintech Fest. Such a platform, she said, should not speak over individual companies but provide the sector with "a credible collective voice internationally".
Sitharaman also hit back at critics who question the sustainability of India's growth, dismissing them as "naraz phuphas" who are never short of reasons to doubt the country's momentum and the capabilities of its young population. She said such critics were debating on television whether India's demographic dividend had slipped away or turned into a burden, relying on "vibecasting", rather than actual numbers. In contrast, she said, young Indians were bypassing the cynicism, building enterprises and demonstrating that the country's demographic advantage was already an "active, unstoppable reality".
Meanwhile, the platform could engage foreign govts and regulators early, before regulatory positions harden and barriers are erected, she said. 
It could also identify areas where standards can remain interoperable, share best practices on data and cybersecurity, and help Indian companies navigate different licensing regimes.
Sitharaman's statement comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for linking India's domestic payment networks with those of other countries. RBI and govt are also keen on enabling cross-border transactions using central bank digital currencies.
Sitharaman said the platform could represent Indian industry in discussions where international rules governing emerging technologies are being shaped. It could also help Indian companies commercialise and monetise their intellectual property across jurisdictions, build partnerships overseas and enter new markets with greater confidence.

briefs.headline: Days after Bhatt, another director quits Coforge board
briefs.deck: Coforge has experienced a shakeup as independent director DK Singh resigns amid tensions over the board’s strategy. His departure follows the resignation of chairman OP Bhatt, sparked by an internal audit that uncovered issues with the evaluation report. The audit revealed that important evaluation findings were not shared with all directors, spotlighting serious governance weaknesses that KPMG…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Boardroom turmoil at Coforge has deepened with independent director and Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) chair DK Singh resigning days after chairman OP Bhatt stepped down amid an internal audit that flagged concerns over how board-evaluation findings were presented to directors.
Singh resigned with immediate effect, citing "differences and tension" between independent and executive directors and concerns over possible changes in strategy, transparency and compensation. His exit comes as the internal audit and governance review, which led the board to seek explanations from both Bhatt and Singh, remains open.Bhatt's resignation followed a KPMG internal audit that flagged procedural lapses in how Coforge's board-evaluation reports were shared with directors, including the withholding of the lowest rating given to the chairman, according to people familiar with the matter.
Boardroom shake-up
The audit found that detailed board-evaluation reports were available only to Bhatt and the NRC chair and were not shared with other directors, including independent directors. The reports were presented to the NRC and board without copies being circulated, the sources said.
More significantly, the chairman's category received the lowest rating in the evaluation, but this was not disclosed or discussed with the NRC or board, they said. 
Calls and text messages to Bhatt did not elicit a response by press time.
The issue surfaced when KPMG reviewed governance processes as part of its Q2 FY26 internal-audit plan. According to the sources, Bhatt instructed the company secretary not to circulate the detailed reports to other directors. The NRC chair subsequently presented the findings jointly with Bhatt at NRC and board meetings, giving the board the impression that the evaluation had produced broadly positive results despite several sections receiving low scores, the sources said.
The development led the board to seek an explanation from Bhatt, who resigned on September 8 before the review was concluded.
In his resignation email dated Sept 10, Singh said the recent events had made it difficult for him to continue discharging his responsibilities at the organisation.
"When I joined the Board in 2024, it was transitioning from a private equity-led Board to a more independent Board. While I believe that transition was moving in the right direction, it also created some differences and tension, particularly between the Independent and Executive Directors," Singh said.

briefs.headline: NSE reduces public offer size to 22.6k crore, issue opens Sept 17
briefs.deck: Bourse's Shares Slotted To Be Listed On BSE On Sept 24
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The much-awaited NSE IPO will open on Sept 17 and close on Sept 21 with the listing slotted for Sept 24, the bourse said on Friday. With some of the existing shareholders together selling a 5.1% stake in the country's largest stock exchange, at the upper end of the Rs 1,700-1,785/share price band, the IPO would be worth Rs 22,568 crore.
At the upper end of the price band, NSE will command a valuation of Rs 4.4 lakh crore, putting it in the league of companies like Hindustan Unilever (current market capitalisation of Rs 4.5 lakh crore), Titan (Rs 4.4 lakh crore) and Sun Pharma (Rs 4.4 lakh crore).
Pocketing multi-bagger returns
In the IPO, a total of 23 NSE shareholders together are selling a little over 12.6 crore shares of the bourse. The selling shareholders include State Bank of India, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Aranda Investments (Mauritius), MS Strategic (Mauritius), The New India Assurance, SBI Capital Markets, Bank of Baroda, Stock Holding Corp of India, General Insurance Corp, and United India Insurance.
At Rs 22,568 crore, NSE's IPO would be the second biggest such offer in India, behind Hyundai India's Rs 27,800-crore IPO that closed towards the end of 2024. Earlier, NSE's IPO was expected to raise about Rs 30,000 crore, which would have made it the largest IPO in India.
On Sept 4, markets regulator Sebi had cleared NSE's IPO documents. During the launch of the bourse's IPO, Ashishkumar Chauhan, CEO & MD, NSE, said that earlier, in the run-up to the offer, some of its existing investors were willing to sell a higher quantum of shares in the IPO. 
But closer to the launch of the offer, some shareholders expressed their willingness to part with a lesser number of NSE shares.
Those shareholders may have done so in expectation of some upside in the future, Chauhan said. When asked about the price band for the IPO, Chauhan said that it was decided by the merchant bankers who are advising the bourse. "After deliberations and roadshows across the world, our merchant bankers have advised us that this is the price," he said.
The shares of NSE will be listed only on BSE since Sebi doesn't allow self-listing, meaning an exchange cannot list its own shares on its trading platform. Likewise, BSE is traded only on NSE.
However, there's a provision of 'permitted to trade' segment on the bourses. Under this category, even if a stock is not listed, the bourse could allow it to trade on its platform. When asked, Chauhan said that NSE has not written to the regulator to explore such an option for NSE shares to get traded on its own platform.
Some of the early investors in NSE, all PSUs, are making up to 5,578 times return in the offer.
On Friday, in the unofficial market for stocks, the grey market premium (GMP), the mark-up the NSE stocks could command on listing over the offer price, was Rs 218 per share, indicating a listing price of Rs 2,003. Depending on market conditions and investors' response to an IPO, GMP keeps fluctuating till the time of listing.

briefs.headline: RBI moves to suck out excess liquidity
briefs.deck: As Forex Reserves Swell To All-Time High Of $786Bn, RBI Announces Sale Of 1L Cr Bonds
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The $136.4 billion raised by banks from non-residents and foreign lenders, then swapped with RBI, has swelled India's foreign-exchange reserves by a record $44.9 billion to $785.7 billion in the week ended Sept 4. The windfall gives RBI a larger war chest to defend the rupee, but creates a problem at home with too much cash in the banking system.
RBI is now trying to mop up that liquidity. On Friday, it announced a Rs 1 lakh crore open-market sale of govt bonds, turning a successful foreign-currency fund-raising exercise into a domestic liquidity-management headache.RBI will sell Rs 1 lakh crore of govt bonds maturing in FY29-32 in three tranches on Sept 17, 21 and 28 to drain surplus liquidity. This is its first net bond sale in two years. Bond yields rose after the announcement, with the 10-year yield up six basis points to 7.04% and the five-year yield nearly 10 basis points to 6.62%.
Highest weekly increases
Banks raised $127 billion through the special forex mobilisation scheme, creating surplus rupee liquidity and pushing overnight rates below the repo rate. Markets had expected measures including FX swaps, MSS bonds, OMO sales and a possible CRR hike.
Exploring oprions: RBI
In an interview with a TV channel, RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said the central bank had several options to manage liquidity beyond VRRR, including open market operations and FX swaps. He said "nothing is off the table." RBI has also been using dollar-rupee swaps to reduce banks' rupee holdings. FCNR(B) deposits mobilised through the recently concluded RBI swap facility totalled $127.2 billion. Malhotra said the flows were "very robust" and reflected strong investor confidence in India's macroeconomic fundamentals. He said the exercise showed that foreign capital could be mobilised within a short period and strengthened financial stability and external sector resilience.
He also said the inflows had helped stabilise the forex market. "It has given us the liquidity at the same time, and it has improved sentiments," he said. Nearly half of the deposits, or around 48.5-50%, have a five-year tenure. About 42% fall in the three-to-four-year maturity bracket and around 9% in the four-to-five-year window. Some of the liquidity will be withdrawn automatically over time, he said. Higher crude prices remain a risk to inflation.
Eye on inflation
Malhotra said the impact would depend on the extent to which higher costs are passed through. "Crude has gone up. July was for the Indian basket an average of $82 (per barrel). Aug it has gone up to $90 (per barrel) and so that will certainly have some impact, but it will depend again on the pass-through," he said.
Malhotra said govt had absorbed and cushioned much of the oil shock, helping the economy weather the impact. RBI will continue to watch inflation persistence, expectations and generalisation ahead of the next monetary policy committee meeting on Oct 5-7. "I mean, risks are there on both sides... The MPC will make a reassessment of the growth-inflation dynamics when it meets in a month or so. Let me not give my assessment," he said.

briefs.headline: India-EU FTA draft: European cars, wine, farm goods set for lower tariffs; key changes explained
briefs.bodyText:
European carmakers will get a significantly wider opening to India’s passenger vehicle market under the proposed India-EU free trade agreement, with the draft pact released on Friday providing for concessional import duties on up to 1 lakh cars in the first year. The quota will gradually rise to 1.6 lakh vehicles from the 10th year of implementation.
The draft text provides tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for EU-origin internal-combustion engine (ICE) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), with the concessional duty linked to the vehicle’s CIF value. The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of this year and could come into force next year, reported PTI.
What changes for EU cars
The concessions will apply only to passenger vehicles priced at Euro 15,000 (around Rs 16.6 lakh) or more. Cars below that threshold will continue to face the existing tariff.
For vehicles priced between Euro 15,000 and Euro 35,000 (around Rs 16.6 lakh to Rs 38.8 lakh), the in-quota duty will fall from 110 per cent to 35 per cent in the first year and then to 10 per cent by the fifth year.
For cars priced above Euro 35,000, the duty will fall from the existing most-favoured-nation tariff of 66 per cent to 30 per cent in the first year and eventually to 10 per cent.
The overall quota for ICE and hybrid passenger cars will rise from 1 lakh units in the first year to 1.07 lakh in the second year, 1.15 lakh in the third, 1.225 lakh in the fourth and 1.3 lakh in the fifth year. It will then increase progressively to 1.6 lakh vehicles from the 10th year.
From the fifth year, 43,000 vehicles will be reserved for cars priced above Euro 50,000 (around Rs 55.4 lakh).
India will also gradually lower tariffs on EU cars imported outside the quota. For cars priced between Euro 15,000 and Euro 50,000, the out-of-quota duty will eventually fall to 35 per cent by the 10th year, while the duty on cars priced above Euro 50,000 will fall to 30 per cent.
The pact also provides a separate quota for completely knocked-down ICE and hybrid vehicles. The quota will stand at 75,000 units annually for the first five years before gradually declining to 50,000 units from the 10th year. The in-quota duty will fall from 13.75 per cent in the first year to 8.25 per cent from the third year, against the current 16.5 per cent.
EVs, wine and farm products
Concessions for battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and other eligible technologies will begin from the fifth year. They will apply only to vehicles priced at Euro 20,000 (around Rs 22 lakh) or more.
The CBU quota for these vehicles will start at 20,000 units in the fifth year, rise to 50,000 in the 10th year and reach 90,000 from the 14th year onwards. The in-quota duty will fall from 30 per cent in the fifth year to 10 per cent in the 10th year, compared with the listed base duty of 110 per cent. Vehicles below the Euro 20,000 price threshold will not receive the concession.
The draft pact also offers tariff concessions on selected EU agricultural and food products, including wine, pork, apples, kiwifruit, pears and peaches, largely through quotas and price-based conditions.
For wine, products valued below Euro 2.50 per 750 ml will receive no concession and will continue to face the 150 per cent base customs duty. Wine priced between Euro 2.50 and Euro 10 will see the duty fall to 75 per cent in the first year and to 30 per cent from the eighth year. For wine priced at Euro 10 or more, the duty will progressively fall to 20 per cent from the eighth year.
India will also allow 2,000 metric tonnes of EU pork annually at concessional rates, while the quota for apples will start at 50,000 tonnes and rise to 1 lakh tonnes from the 11th year, subject to a minimum CIF price of Rs 80 per kg.
The first-year quota for kiwifruit will be 12,000 tonnes, rising to 15,000 tonnes from the 11th year. Pears will have a fixed annual quota of 2,250 tonnes, while the quota for peaches will be limited to 20 tonnes a year.
GTRI flags wider implications
The concessions mark a significant opening of some of India’s sensitive markets under the proposed FTA.
GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said the EU had become the second major trade partner after the UK to secure automotive tariff concessions from India under an FTA.
“Having established these precedents, India should soon receive similar demands for preferential market access and generous TRQs from other key trade partners such as Japan and South Korea,” he said.
Srivastava noted that India imported only 17,191 cars from the EU in 2025, while the agreement provides European automakers with a first-year quota of 1 lakh completely built-up ICE and non-plug-in hybrid cars.
“That is almost six times current imports,” he said.
He said India had opened parts of several sensitive markets through tariff-rate quotas and price-based concessions rather than unrestricted tariff cuts.
“These commitments cover automobiles, wine and selected alcoholic products, pork, apples, kiwifruit, pears and peaches. Imports meeting the prescribed origin, price and quantity conditions will enter at lower duties, while most imports outside these limits will continue to face the normal tariff,” he said.

briefs.headline: MPC will reassess growth-inflation dynamics at next meeting: RBI Governor
briefs.deck: On inflation, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the rising crude oil prices will have an impact but it will depend on how much is passed through
briefs.bodyText:
“Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will reassess growth and inflation dynamics at its meeting next month amid rising prices of crude oil owing to the ongoing West Asia crisis,” Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Friday (September 11, 2026).
In an interview to CNBC-TV18, the Governor also said nearly 50% of the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B) deposits, mobilised under the forex swap facility is for 5-year tenor. The inflows under the FCNR(B) deposits totalled $127.22 billion in the recently concluded RBI swap facility.
On inflation, Mr. Malhotra said the rising crude oil prices will have an impact but it will depend on how much is passed through.
"Crude has gone up. July was for the Indian basket an average of $82 (per barrel). August it has gone up to $90 (per barrel) and so that will certainly have some impact, but it will depend again on the pass-through," Mr. Malhotra said in the interview.
According to him, the government has to a great degree absorbed and cushioned that shock, as a result of that the Indian economy has weathered this shock really well. The RBI Governor said it would continue to watch whether there is persistence, inflation expectations, and generalisation.
"I mean, risks are there on both sides... The MPC will make a reassessment of the growth-inflation dynamics when it meets in a month or so. Let me not give my assessment," he said. The next meeting of the MPC, the RBI's rate-setting panel, is scheduled for October 5-7, 2026.
On FCNR(B) deposits, the Governor said the flows were certainly "very robust" and reflect the strong belief and confidence of the investors worldwide in the extremely strong macroeconomic fundamentals of India.
"It demonstrates at the same time that we can get foreign flows, capital flows, in a short period of time. This helps us, in terms of financial stability, external sector resilience. We are quite happy with the result," he added. Mr. Malhotra said the strong flows has helped stabilise the forex markets. "It has given us the liquidity at the same time, and it has improved sentiments," he said.
He said that FCNR(B) deposits are predominantly concentrated in the 5-year tenure, which accounts for nearly half of the total portfolio at approximately (48.50-50%).
The next largest segment, comprising about 42%, falls within the 3-year up to 4-year maturity bracket. The remaining share, about 9%, falls in 4-5 years' tenure window.
Mr. Malhotra said the Reserve Bank has enough tools at its disposal to manage the current surplus of liquidity in the banking system, and is prepared to use them as needed. “Some of the liquidity will be withdrawn on its own over a period of time,” he added.

stories.headline: Zverev beats Khachanov, reaches US Open final and eyes second major of year
stories.deck: Alexander Zverev battled his way to the US Open final, showcasing resilience in a gripping match. Having triumphed at the French Open earlier this year, he now faces an American in the championship, a historic moment as the U.S. has lacked a men's Grand Slam champion since 2003. This final is a crucial chance for Zverev to cement his legacy with another prestigious title.
stories.bodyText:
Alexander Zverev has spent years knowing the frustration of coming close to a Grand Slam title without being able to finish the job. After finally ending that wait at the French Open this year, the German now has another major opportunity in front of him.
This time, though, he is hoping to extend an even longer drought.
Zverev reached the US Open final on Friday with a 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6) victory over Karen Khachanov, setting up a Sunday showdown against either No. 8 seed Ben Shelton or No. 11 Frances Tiafoe.
Neither Shelton nor Tiafoe has previously reached a Grand Slam final, although both have made it to the US Open semifinals. The winner of their clash will be bidding to become the first American man to play for the title in New York.
The United States is still waiting for its next men's Grand Slam champion, with Andy Roddick's US Open triumph in 2003 remaining the country's most recent men's major title.
"Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday," Zverev said.
Zverev's long wait finally ends
For much of his career, Zverev carried the unwanted tag of being the best men's player without a Grand Slam title. That changed at the French Open this year when he finally claimed his first major.
The 24-2 record he has compiled in Grand Slam matches this season underlines just how dramatically his fortunes have changed.
After winning in Paris, Zverev went on to reach the Wimbledon final, where he was beaten by Jannik Sinner. He now has a chance to add another major title only months after breaking through for the first time.
"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I’ve had a lot of struggles at the major level, I was so close so many times, and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.
2020 heartbreak still fresh
A US Open title would carry particular significance for Zverev because of what happened five years ago.
In the 2020 final, he appeared to be on course for his maiden Grand Slam crown after taking the opening two sets against Dominic Thiem. But Thiem fought back and eventually prevailed in a fifth-set tiebreak.
That victory made Thiem the first man since 1949 to win the US Open after losing the opening two sets.
Zverev now has another chance to finish the job in New York.
Against Khachanov, he made sure the match did not follow the same pattern. After taking the first two sets, he stayed composed and closed out the contest in straight sets. The victory also extended his run to 13 consecutive sets won.
Khachanov fights back but Zverev holds firm
Khachanov entered the semifinal as the No. 50-ranked player and was chasing an unexpected run to his first Grand Slam final.
The Russian had arrived in New York with a losing record for the season but produced one of the tournament's surprise campaigns to reach his third Grand Slam semifinal and his second at the US Open.
He struggled initially against Zverev, losing the first set and then falling 2-0 behind in the second. But he gradually found his rhythm, broke Zverev's serve to level the set and stayed with the top seed until the tiebreak.
Khachanov saved Zverev's first two set points, but the German eventually prevailed after winning a remarkable 34-shot rally.
The third set again went to a tiebreak, and Khachanov looked well placed after moving 3-0 and then 5-2 ahead.
Zverev, however, produced another comeback to deny him and seal his place in the final.
Rocky start before a run to the final
Zverev's path to the championship match has been far from straightforward.
He became the first No. 1-seeded man to play five-set matches in each of the opening two rounds of a major after being pushed the distance by Lorenzo Sonego and Quentin Halys.
Those two matches alone kept him on court for nearly 9 1/2 hours. Zverev admitted that his performances were poor enough for him and his team to laugh about them after his second-round match.
"That kind of sense of humor, it helped me," Zverev said.
The German gradually turned things around as the tournament progressed.
"Moving forward, I was playing much better tennis. Obviously I have improved a little bit. Otherwise, I wouldn’t be in the U.S. Open final."
While Zverev and Khachanov battled for a place in the final, the other semifinal was expected to command much of the attention in New York.
Shelton and Tiafoe, two of the biggest fan favourites in American men's tennis, were due to meet on a day that also marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.
Both players had already reached the US Open semifinals before, but neither had managed to go one step further at a Grand Slam.
The winner would not only reach a maiden major final but also keep alive America's hopes of ending its long wait for a men's Grand Slam champion.
Interestingly, the Zverev-Khachanov semifinal had attracted surprisingly low ticket prices compared with the Shelton-Tiafoe contest. Khachanov, ranked No. 50, was also attempting to become the lowest-ranked US Open finalist since the ATP rankings began in 1973.
Zverev, however, made sure the Russian's remarkable run ended one match short of the final.

Zverev finally broke through at the French Open this year and followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, where he lost to Jannik Sinner. The German is 24-2 in Grand Slam matches this season.
“Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I’ve had a lot of struggles at the major level, I was so close so many times, and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court,” Zverev said.
Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the U.S. Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.
Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first No. 1-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.
Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third Grand Slam semifinal, including second at the U.S. Open.
He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev’s serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.
Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.

stories.headline: Mbappé On Viral Dictator Memes: Real Madrid star says jokes cross a line
stories.deck: Kylian Mbappé has addressed the viral memes portraying him as a dictator, admitting some are funny but saying comparisons to figures responsible for mass suffering cross a line. The Real Madrid and France star also discussed teammate Ousmane Dembélé’s “Mobutu” nickname, which he takes more lightly, while continuing to enjoy a strong start to the new season.
stories.bodyText:
Kylian Mbappé has never been short of attention, but a strange social-media trend surrounding the France and Real Madrid star has taken his fame in a direction he would rather not embrace. Images of Mbappé dressed as a dictator, sitting on a throne and appearing alongside some of history’s most controversial political figures have spread online, turning his footballing influence into the unlikely subject of a viral meme.
The 27-year-old can see the joke behind it, but he also believes there is a line that should not be crossed when the humour involves people responsible for immense suffering. Mbappé addressed the trend while reflecting on the way social media can turn almost anything involving a high-profile footballer into a running joke.
For him, the problem is not simply being mocked or given an exaggerated nickname. It is the historical weight attached to the figures he is being compared with.
Mbappé explains why he is uncomfortable with the dictator comparisons
The origin of the meme remains unclear. One possible explanation links it to Mbappé’s decision to sue a kebab shop owner in 2024 over the use of his name in the description of a sandwich.
Others have speculated that the images are a joke about the level of influence Mbappé has reportedly wielded at Real Madrid and previously at Paris Saint-Germain.
The memes have taken several forms. Mbappé has been portrayed wearing military uniforms, sitting on a throne and standing alongside controversial historical leaders, including Soviet leader Josef Stalin.
Speaking to L’Équipe, Mbappé acknowledged that some people clearly intend the images as harmless fun. However, he said the comparisons become uncomfortable because of the real-world consequences associated with the people being referenced.
“It is in part funny because you get the sense that, for some people, it's all in good fun,” Mbappé said.
“But there is also the part that is not so funny, because we know the damage this genre of people have caused throughout history.”
Mbappé was particularly uncomfortable with being compared with people responsible for mass suffering.
“To be compared to people who murder others, or who have caused misery for millions and millions of people ... I don't think I've ever done anything like that in my life. So there's a mix of things.”
The France international added that he understands the light-hearted intention behind the trend, but believes it can also reveal something about the people sharing it.
“On the one hand, I know it's done in a lighthearted way and it isn't meant to be taken too far, but it perhaps shows a lack of political and human awareness in people.”
Dembélé’s “Mobutu” nickname is a different kind of joke
The subject also brought up a nickname given to Mbappé by his France teammate Ousmane Dembélé: “Mobutu”.
The name refers to Mobutu Sese Seko, the former dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, which he renamed Zaire, from 1965 until 1997.
Mbappé appeared to take that particular joke much more lightly.
“Ousmane, he is something different,” Mbappé said with a smile. “He found it on social media! He's just having a laugh.”
The meme discussion comes as Mbappé continues to make headlines for considerably more conventional reasons on the pitch. The France captain has started the 2026-27 season strongly for Real Madrid, scoring five goals in his first five games of the campaign.
He is next due to feature on Saturday night when José Mourinho’s side host Rayo Vallecano.

stories.headline: Jose Mourinho’s latest sermon: Jude Bellingham as gospel
stories.deck: The Portuguese has long been described as a reactionary coach. But every great side he has built — from Porto to Chelsea to Inter Milan to Real Madrid — has had a creative genius at its heart. Can the ‘Special One’ replicate the script with Jude Bellingham in his second stint in the Spanish capital?
stories.bodyText:
Parking the bus. That’s the verdict history has handed down on Jose Mourinho – repeated so often that it has calcified into fact. It’s like a half-truth, enough to make it stick, but never quite enough to make it whole.
But Mourinho has worn it the way a magician wears a top hat: perfectly tailored, endlessly convenient, and never, not for one second, the whole trick.
Call him defensive, and you have only named the shadow he casts, not the man casting it. His teams defend well not because attack frightens him, but because chaos does. Evidently, in a Mourinho side, nothing is left to chance, more so when the motions of the game have already strangled every other variable into submission.
Pragmatism is the colder, harder word – less quotable and less fun to chant from the grandstands. So the easier opinion has survived instead, passed down like folklore.
ALSO READ | Messi and Argentina: A legacy that will stand the test of time
Just as false is the myth that his touchline is where creativity goes to die – a graveyard for gifted men. Every successful Mourinho side has had one player built into its architecture so completely that the team’s pulse becomes indistinguishable from his own.
Deco did not wither at FC Porto. Mesut Ozil did not shrink at Real Madrid. Wesley Sneijder did not dim at Inter Milan. Eidur Gudjohnsen and Oscar were not sacrificed on some altar of defensive orthodoxy at Chelsea. The names change, the pattern doesn’t.
That graveyard, as it turns out, was never there. Detractors simply needed it to exist, and told the story so many times that absence began to look like proof.
Elevating the whole
And now, in the early light of his second reign in the Spanish capital – a squad glittering with names built for newspaper headlines and highlight reels – Mourinho has once again refused the obvious altar.
The Portuguese is neither building his cathedral around Kylian Mbappe’s blistering speed nor around Vinicius Junior’s dazzling, unpredictable chaos, talented as both unquestionably are.
The ‘Special One’ is building it around Jude Bellingham. Because, when Bellingham ticks, Madrid ticks with him.
Mourinho did not ease the 23-year-old in gently. Just a week after he rejoined the squad following an extended break granted to Madrid’s World Cup contingent, the Englishman started centrally in the season-opener against Espanyol, pushing Bernardo Silva deeper and shifting Arda Guler wider.
If Bellingham was short of match fitness, it never showed. Everything coherent Madrid did that afternoon ran through him, like current through a wire. That he broke the deadlock himself, registering the first goal of Mourinho’s Madrid comeback, only made the script sweeter.
Mourinho has found a structure that lets Bellingham defend without shackling his attacking instincts, and the early signs are quite validating: two goals and as many assists from four league games, another goal directly created and the post rattled for good measure.
“He is a unique and extremely important player, one with diverse talents, from physical to mental and tactical. He also has the ability to win back possession, press effectively and score goals, especially in the air. He is an absolutely impressive player,” Mourinho gushed ahead of the contest against Malaga. In the 4-0 win, Bellingham scored one and assisted one.
Leading by example
Bellingham is the first Madrid player to contribute to at least four goals through the opening three matches of a league campaign since – fittingly – he himself did it, managing four goals and one assist upon first arriving on Spanish shores back in 2023. In fact, he had become the first Real Madrid player to score in each of his first four games since Cristiano Ronaldo in 2009.
The numbers are starting to rhyme with the ones that made him a phenomenon in the first place.
ALSO READ | Who will seize control of the post-Pep Premier League era?
But this tells only a part of the Bellingham story. He has been among Madrid’s leading players in ball recoveries, chance creation and successful passes in the opposition half. He is helping Los Blancos progress possession, break lines, and win duels in the midfield. He presses like a man late for something urgent, creates like an artist with time to spare, and yet arrives in the box to finish the moves he himself started.
Here, there, everywhere
He is omnipresent on the pitch – at the shoulder of every teammate like a ghostly butler anticipating a need before it’s spoken, or hounding opponents like a sweat-inducing nightmare they can’t quite wake up from.
“Now I play with a bit more freedom, with the liberty to move further up or down the pitch, depending on our needs. I’m having a lot of fun, I’m really enjoying my football, and that’s why I’m performing well,” he declared after the triumph over Malaga.
In simple terms, what Mourinho is attempting is a kind of resurrection: coaxing back the version of Bellingham last seen in 2023-24, the one which scored 23 goals and set up 13 more in an astounding debut season.
England, for its part, would attest that the lad from the Midlands is at his most dangerous when he is at the centre of a team’s creative output – witness seven goals and an assist in eight matches at this summer’s World Cup, once he was finally deployed where he belonged.
And Madrid needs this every bit as much as Mourinho. The club must start restocking its trophy cabinet, so must he, for this is his last chance saloon. That he is building Madrid’s future, and staking his own claim to a prolonged, top-of-the-line managerial career, around Bellingham is not really a decision. It’s a no-brainer dressed up as a gamble.
The new main event
Madrid’s road ahead is no procession. Barcelona is playing like it has found a cheat code – seventeen goals scored already, and only two conceded. The fight for European glory looks no gentler, even if it began well enough with a 2-1 win over Inter Milan.
But if Madrid intends to mount serious title challenges on all fronts, it will need Bellingham to continue doing exactly what he’s doing now: running havoc from defense to attack, box to box, whistle to whistle.
The boy who once copied Brazilian Ronaldo’s Cascao haircut at Birmingham City FC could have grown up to be a footnote in someone else’s Real Madrid era – a talented supporting player orbiting Mbappe’s brilliance or Vinicius’ fireworks.
ALSO READ | Parkinson’s Law, Butterfly Effect, and the beautiful chaos of deadline day
But while Mbappe provides the spectacle and Vinicius the hustle, Bellingham provides the architecture. And architecture, in the end, is what outlasts everything else.
‘Hey Jude’ – that classic Beatles soundtrack of his debut season – had gone quiet last year, muffled under a run of injuries. Now, the Madrid faithful are singing it again, and for good reason. This, after all, is Bellingham’s team. He is not a supporting act dressed up in superstar company. He is the main attraction.
Mourinho spent more than 20 years making sure the story was always about him. Perhaps the last great plot twist is that he’s letting it be about someone else this time.

briefs.headline: Women's Asia Cup: Sri Lanka fight back from 33/4 to beat Pakistan, set up India final
briefs.deck: Sri Lanka emerged victorious in a dramatic four-wicket win against Pakistan during the Women's Asia Cup semi-final. Despite a rocky start, they rallied impressively to chase down the target. Fatima Sana, Pakistan's captain, delivered a commendable performance, yet her efforts fell short. This thrilling victory sets the stage for Sri Lanka to challenge India in the forthcoming tournament finale.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Defending champions Sri Lanka produced a remarkable fightback under pressure to beat Pakistan by four wickets and book their place in the Women’s Asia Cup final, where they will face India in a repeat of the 2024 summit clash.
Chasing 131 at the Dubai International Stadium on Friday, Sri Lanka slumped to 33/4 inside seven overs before Harshitha Samarawickrama and Kavisha Dilhari launched a stirring recovery. The pair added 67 runs for the fifth wicket to bring Sri Lanka within touching distance of victory.
Pakistan captain Fatima Sana briefly reignited her side’s hopes by dismissing both batters in the 17th over, leaving Sri Lanka at 109/6 and still needing 22 runs from the final three overs. But Nilakshika Silva and Kaushani Nuthyangana held their nerve to finish the chase with eight balls to spare.
Sri Lanka reached 131/6 in 18.4 overs, with Nilakshika unbeaten on 18 off 10 balls and Nuthyangana 10 not out from four deliveries.
Harshitha, Dilhari rescue Sri Lanka
Pakistan had made a competitive 130/5 after being asked to bat first. They too had endured a difficult start, slipping to 52/4 inside 10 overs before Fatima Sana’s unbeaten 47 off 36 balls helped revive the innings.
Shawaal Zulfiqar provided early momentum with a 24 off 16 balls, while Gull Feroza made 21. But Sri Lanka’s bowlers kept Pakistan under pressure, with Chamari Athapaththu and Chamudi Praboda taking two wickets apiece and Sugandika Kumari claiming one.
Sri Lanka’s chase then appeared to be heading towards trouble when Fatima removed Athapaththu and Sanjana Kavindi with successive deliveries in the second over. Hasini Perera and Imesha Dulani also fell quickly, leaving the defending champions four down.
Harshitha and Dilhari changed the complexion of the chase with their 67-run stand. Harshitha made 36 from 31 balls, while Dilhari scored 33 off 33, repeatedly finding singles and rotating the strike to absorb the pressure.
“The way Harshitha and Kavisha batted, it's amazing. They absorbed the pressure, they took singles and played really good. Under pressure, that partnership was match winning,” Sri Lanka captain Athapaththu said after the game.
Fatima, who was named Player of the Match for her 4/38 and unbeaten 47, struck again to remove both set batters. But Pakistan could not close out the game.
“Most of the things went well, but the last bit, (the) Sri Lankan middle order took the game away,” Fatima said. “I think the way Harshitha and Kavisha played... They are good in (taking) singles. So credit goes to them.”
Repeat of 2024 final awaits
The victory takes Sri Lanka into their third consecutive Women’s Asia Cup final. They will once again face India, who defeated Bangladesh by 40 runs in their semi-final and have remained unbeaten in the tournament.
Sri Lanka defeated India by eight wickets in the 2024 final to claim their maiden Asia Cup title. India, meanwhile, will be chasing a record-extending eighth crown when the two sides meet on Sunday.
Athapaththu believes Sri Lanka have enough depth to challenge India again.
“We have good finishers like Harshitha, Nilakshika, Kavisha. Most of the players are playing really good, even the bowling unit. So we have good players. So if we can execute our plans in the final, I think we can beat any team,” she said.
For Pakistan, the defeat ended their campaign after an inconsistent tournament, while Sri Lanka’s ability to recover from 33/4 once again underlined the resilience that has taken them back to the Asia Cup final.

briefs.headline: Pakistan mount stunning fightback, force tricky chase for England at Edgbaston
briefs.deck: Day 3 of the third Test brought a thrilling turn of events as Pakistan demonstrated their resilience with a phenomenal 449 runs in their second innings, spanning nearly 97 overs. This left England with a target of just 130 runs to clinch the series. The highlight was a crucial 121-run partnership for the ninth wicket that stifled England's bowling attack, setting the stage for an exciting Day 4…
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan produced a remarkable fightback on Day 3 of the third Test at Edgbaston, turning what looked like a straightforward innings defeat into a potentially tricky chase for England.
After being bowled out for just 133 in their first innings and conceding a 320-run lead, Pakistan were expected to fold quickly in their second innings. Instead, they battled for nearly 97 overs and were eventually dismissed for 449, leaving England a target of 130 runs to win the Test and complete a 3-0 series clean sweep.
The result means England will return on Day 4 needing only 130 runs, but Pakistan's extraordinary lower-order resistance ensured the hosts could not finish the match on the third evening.
Masood, Babar and Azan lead Pakistan's fightback
Pakistan's recovery was built around contributions from their top and middle order.
Captain Shan Masood narrowly missed out on a century, scoring a determined 95 to anchor the innings. Azan Awais added 59, while Babar Azam played an assured knock of 76 as Pakistan steadily erased England's huge first-innings advantage.
Just when Pakistan appeared to have done enough to force England to bat again, wickets began to tumble and England sensed another opportunity to wrap up the Test. 
But the lower order had other ideas.
Razaullah and Abbas produce stunning 121-run stand
Debutant Razaullah delivered the biggest surprise of the day with a sensational counter-attacking 81 from 73 balls.
Batting at No. 9, Razaullah took the attack to England's bowlers and struck nine sixes during his entertaining innings. He found an unlikely but hugely valuable partner in Mohammad Abbas, who held his end together as the pair added 121 runs for the ninth wicket.
The partnership stunned England and frustrated their attempts to complete a series sweep on the third day.
England eventually broke the stand when Josh Tongue dismissed Abbas, ending one of the most unexpected partnerships of the Test. Razaullah's innings also came to an end shortly afterwards as England's bowlers finally cleaned up the tail.
Gus Atkinson played a key role in the late breakthroughs, while Jofra Archer and Tongue had earlier kept Pakistan's batters under pressure.
Pakistan's 449 meant England were left with 130 to win. While the target remains modest, the visitors' extraordinary fightback has at least forced England to bat again after their first-innings dominance.
England now have a clear opportunity to complete a 3-0 series victory on Day 4. Pakistan, meanwhile, will hope their lower-order heroics have given them enough momentum to create one final twist in a Test that appeared to be heading towards an early finish.
Brief scores: Pakistan 133 & 449; England 453. England need 130 runs to win.

briefs.headline: Poor show in Sri Lanka due to long break: Siraj
briefs.deck: The pacer believes his rhythm is back, thanks to playing in the Duleep Trophy final
briefs.bodyText:
Following India’s recent Test tour of Sri Lanka, Mohammed Siraj came under scrutiny after an underwhelming performance in the two-match series.
The Hyderabad pacer took just one wicket in each of the four innings. Siraj’s woes continued in the Duleep Trophy final that concluded here on Thursday, where he managed just one wicket in South Zone’s loss to East Zone.
In the first innings of the Duleep final, Siraj was lacklustre, but he came up with an improved effort in the second essay.
“In the first innings, the pitch looked fresh, so I tried to bowl too fast. Because I was forcing it, my rhythm was off. In the second, I told myself to forget the outcome and just run in with good, natural rhythm. The moment I did that, the old Siraj was back in action, and the ball started coming out beautifully,” he said.
Before the Lanka tour, Siraj’s last competitive game was the one-off Test against Afghanistan in June. The 32-year-old said the two-month break was the reason for his poor form.
“Coming off a two-month break straight into a match, my rhythm wasn’t quite there. Heading into this game, my primary goal was to find that flow. Playing this match helped tremendously,” said Siraj.
“After two months off, your body doesn’t react the same way — everything feels a beat slower. Getting through this game got my body moving again and brought my rhythm right back.”
While there is a lot of focus on workload management, Siraj reckoned his body doesn’t need long breaks.
“Every bowler’s body is different, mine doesn’t handle long breaks well. A short breather is fine, but in my career, I had never taken two full months off,” he quipped.
“I was working out in the gym and bowling occasionally, but no amount of practice can replicate match intensity. It was a new experience, but a learning curve for me going forward.”
In the two Tests, Siraj struggled with his pace as well, operating in the 120-130 kph zone and never touching 140 kph.
“I’m purely a rhythm bowler. If I’m not in sync, I can’t explode through the crease. That was the struggle in Sri Lanka — my run-up felt disjointed. Some strides were too short, others were too long, and that broke my flow and cost me pace. Out here, everything clicked, and the pace followed naturally,” he added.

briefs.headline: How a forgotten camera helped 5-time Olympic champion Ian Thorpe escape 9/11
briefs.deck: On September 11, 2001, 18-year-old Australian swimming star Ian Thorpe narrowly avoided visiting the World Trade Center after returning to his hotel for a forgotten camera. Already a five-time Olympic champion and six-time world champion, Thorpe later described the near miss as a “very, very close call” and a moment of fate. His extraordinary swimming career continued with further Olympic and…
briefs.bodyText:
Ian Thorpe was only 18 when a forgotten camera changed the course of one September morning. The Australian swimming sensation was in New York on September 11, 2001, and had planned to visit the observation deck of the World Trade Center. He had already gone for an early morning run, grabbed a coffee and was making his way towards the towers when he realised he had left his camera behind at his hotel.
So Thorpe turned around.
That seemingly insignificant decision meant he was back in his hotel room when the first hijacked plane struck the World Trade Center. What followed changed the world, and Thorpe would later look back on those few minutes as an extraordinary stroke of fate.
“He was probably 20 minutes away from being there,” one of Thorpe’s managers, Frank Turner, told Australian radio.
“He was shocked… a few minutes later and who knows what could have happened?”
Thorpe himself has described the experience as a “very, very close call”, saying that moments like it made him realise “some things were meant to be”. It was a narrow escape that came just weeks after the teenager had produced one of the greatest performances in swimming history.
Ian Thorpe was already a swimming phenomenon before his brush with fate
Thorpe was not simply a promising young swimmer when he arrived in New York. By September 2001, he was already a global sporting star.
Just months earlier, at the 2001 World Championships in Fukuoka, Japan, he had won six gold medals and established four world records. His records came in the men’s 200m freestyle, 400m freestyle, 800m freestyle and Australia’s 800m freestyle relay.
His times were extraordinary: 1:44.06 in the 200m freestyle, 3:40.17 in the 400m, 7:39.16 in the 800m and 7:04.66 as part of Australia’s 800m freestyle relay.
That performance had followed an equally memorable Olympic debut on home soil in Sydney in 2000.
- Gold: 400m freestyle
- Gold: 4x100m freestyle relay, where he anchored Australia to victory in a dramatic finish
- Gold: 4x200m freestyle relay
- Silver: 200m freestyle
- Silver: 4x100m medley relay
By the time Thorpe returned to his hotel room on September 11, then, he was already a five-time Olympic champion.
And his career was only beginning.
Thorpe went on to produce another defining Olympic performance at the 2004 Games in Athens, where he won the men's 200m freestyle in what became known as the “Race of the Century”. He defeated defending champion Pieter van den Hoogenband and American teenager Michael Phelps in one of the most anticipated races of the Games.
He also successfully defended his Olympic title in the 400m freestyle, edging fellow Australian Grant Hackett, while adding silver in the 800m freestyle relay and bronze in the 100m freestyle.
His international résumé continued to grow. Thorpe won another three World Championship titles in 2003, while a year earlier he had set a world record of 3:40.08 in the 400m freestyle at the 2002 Commonwealth Games.
That mark was only surpassed in 2009, when Germany’s Paul Biedermann went 0.01 seconds faster in a high-tech super-suit. Thorpe’s time remains the fastest 400m freestyle ever recorded in a textile suit.
He ultimately retired in 2006 after withdrawing from the Commonwealth Games because of bronchitis. Five years later, he attempted a comeback with the goal of qualifying for the 2012 London Olympics, but fell short at the Australian Olympic Trials.
His life after elite swimming has also remained closely connected to issues beyond sport. Thorpe has advocated for same-sex marriage in Australia and spoken openly about his struggles with depression and the difficulties he experienced navigating life as an elite athlete as a gay man. In 2017, he presented a two-part documentary examining the effects of bullying.
But when Thorpe thinks back to September 11, the extraordinary list of medals and records is not what makes that morning remarkable.
He had been in New York with plans to see the World Trade Center. He had intended to visit it with a friend, Michelle, who was staying with him. Instead, Thorpe was the one who went down alone, realised he had forgotten his camera and turned back.
24 years after dramatic 9/11 birth, Maine mother and retired firefighter reunite
“I went down there on the morning of 9/11,” Thorpe recalled. “It was early in the morning and I went for a run. I grabbed a coffee and walked back to my hotel room, and literally in that period of time the planes hit.”
“It was a very, very close call.”
Thorpe later said he and his friend had talked about visiting the World Trade Center in the morning and the Empire State Building at night.
Instead, a forgotten camera sent him back to his hotel at almost exactly the moment his plans needed to change.
“I said to a friend we could go up the World Trade Center in the morning and then you do the Empire State Building at night,” Thorpe said. “But in the end, I was the one that went down there. With things like that, you realize it’s fate. Some things were meant to be, and I realize I am very lucky.”

briefs.headline: GCL: Pipers, Grandmasters inch closer to summit clash
briefs.bodyText:
Magnus Carlsen showed his magnanimous side on Friday. The World No. 1 was presented with the Player-of-the-Match trophy after Alpine APL Pipers scored a crucial win against Fyers American Gambits at the Lalit Ashok.
He, however, handed over the trophy to his teammate Vidit Gujrathi, crediting the Grandmaster from Nashik for the 9-7 victory in the match between the two top teams at the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League.
Carlsen, who beat Javokhir Sindarov, said: “In my game, I was doing pretty well early on but Sindarov put up a good fight. I was able to wriggle out and find the win. As much as I am happy with my win, I don’t deserve the award as much as the man who won us the match.”
That statement was greeted with loud applause by the crowd. Vidit said he was honoured by Carlsen’s gesture.
The five-time World champion wasn’t the only one who was feeling generous on this day. Ganges Grandmasters’ Stavroula Tsolakidou was named the Player-of-the-Match for her win against Carissa Yip of Cheq Mumba Masters. She, however, presented the trophy to the team’s coach B. Adhiban.
The Grandmasters romped home 16-1, with five of the six players winning their games. Going into the final day of the league phase, they have 18 points, the same as the Pipers. But the Grandmasters have 88 points, six more than the Pipers.
The two franchises are inching closer to the final, with only the American Gambits, who are on 15 match points, having an outside chance, but it is not in their hands alone.

briefs.headline: Bumrah finds his rhythm against Sooryavanshi
briefs.bodyText:
In this year’s IPL, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi had left jaws on the floor when he nonchalantly deposited Jasprit Bumrah over mid-on for a six off the first ball he faced from the ace pacer.
On Friday, under lights at the Arun Jaitley Stadium, another glimpse of the box-office duel between the precocious teen and seasoned operator was on view. This came in a mere practice session for the Indian team ahead of the first T20I against Afghanistan on Sunday, but the intensity of the battle was enchanting nevertheless. Sooryavanshi and Bumrah haven’t yet featured for India together.
Sooryavanshi had to be fairly measured on Friday evening, for Bumrah hit his straps and tested the young left-hander with the lengths that he found. The 32-year-old beat Sooryavanshi all ends up on one occasion with a peach on a good length, and also nailed his yorkers most of the time. Sooryavanshi wasn’t fazed, however, as he unfurled a delightful punch off the back foot later.
For Bumrah, it was largely about finding his groove after an injury layoff. He had hurt his left knee during the ODI series against England in July, and had failed to recover in time for the recent Test series versus Sri Lanka. He bowled in the nets for nearly 45 minutes.
The training stint was attended by the entire 15-member squad. After a light drizzle, India was in buoyant mood as it started with elaborate fielding drills. With fielding coach Subhadeep Ghosh, who took over from T. Dilip in August, encouraging the players with the enthusiasm of a recent hire, flat and high catches as well as ground fielding were practised rigorously.
If greater emphasis on the fielding seemed noticeable, it may be to address India’s sloppiness on the tour of the United Kingdom in June-July. A number of catches were spilled as Shreyas Iyer & Co. suffered series defeats to both Ireland and England.

briefs.headline: Jasprit Bumrah bowls in full-squad practice as India step up Afghanistan T20I preparations
briefs.deck: Jasprit Bumrah joined India’s full-squad training session ahead of their three-match T20I series against Afghanistan. The players went through warm-ups, fielding drills and an extended net session. Ishan Kishan briefly raised concerns after going down, but later walked off without apparent discomfort.
briefs.bodyText:
Jasprit Bumrah
 was back in the thick of India’s preparations on Friday as the full squad took part in a training session ahead of the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan.
The session started quietly, with the players going through a light warm-up before moving into fielding drills. Ten players were then split into two groups of five, with the players working in pairs and taking turns trying to hit the stumps.
The intensity picked up once the team moved to the nets. Two nets were in use, with the spinners operating at one end and the seamers at the other.
Ishan Kishan and Shreyas Iyer spent time facing the spin group, which included Washington Sundar, Varun Chakaravarthy, Axar Patel and Ravi Bishnoi. At the other net, Sanju Samson and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi faced the pace attack, with Arshdeep Singh, Shivam Dube, Nitish Kumar Reddy and Bumrah among those bowling.
Axar and Shivam Dube later got their opportunity with the bat, with a few bowlers from Delhi also stepping in to help India get through the evening net session.
The only worrying moment came when Ishan Kishan faced 
Navdeep Saini
. The left-hander tried to duck under a rising delivery, but appeared to get caught awkwardly and went down clutching his lower back. 
He was immediately looked at by the physio.
After spending some time with the medical staff, Kishan was able to walk off the ground on his own. He did not appear to be in obvious discomfort as he left the practice area.
The session was part of India's build-up to their T20I series against Afghanistan. The two sides will meet on September 13, 15 and 17, with all three games to take place at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi.

briefs.headline: 20 runs in 6 innings: Pak openers register worst Test series in 35 years vs England
briefs.deck: In a dismal display, Pakistan's opening batsmen faltered throughout their recent Test series against England, accumulating a mere twenty runs across six partnerships. This represented the team's worst performance in thirty-five years, with no partnership exceeding ten runs. Despite the collective shortcomings, Azan Awais managed to find some consistency, although his partners repeatedly fell…
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan's opening batters endured a disastrous Test series against England, combining for just 20 runs across six opening partnerships in the three-match series, their joint-worst performance in 35 years. The latest failure came in the third Test at Edgbaston, where Pakistan's opening pair was dismissed without adding a run to the scoreboard in the second innings.
The 20-run aggregate is Pakistan's lowest for an opening partnership across a Test series since their home series against the West Indies in 1990-91.
Three opening combinations, no 10-run stand
Pakistan tried three different opening combinations during the series, but none managed to produce even a double-digit stand.
Across six innings, Pakistan's openers managed just 20 runs, with their best opening stand being only eight runs.
Awais fights alone at the top
Azan Awais was the only Pakistan opener to offer any consistency during the series. The youngster scored 129 runs in six innings at an average of 21.50, but received almost no support from his partners. Imam-ul-Haq managed scores of 42 and 0, Shan Masood made 1 and 26, while Saim Ayub returned 0 and 0 in his two innings as an opener.
The repeated early dismissals left Pakistan's middle order under pressure almost immediately.
Another unwanted record at Edgbaston
Pakistan's problems at the top were part of a much wider batting collapse in the third Test. In the first innings at Edgbaston, Pakistan were bowled out for just 133, with their top five batters all dismissed for single-digit scores. It was the first time a team had lost all of its top five wickets for single-digit scores in the first innings of a Test in England.
